subject: Banking
title: Algorithmic Trading in Banks
description: A quick, practical guide to Algorithmic Trading in Banks.

hook.text: Goldman Sachs had 600 equity traders in 2000. By 2020, only 2 remained. Algorithms replaced 598 humans.

buildup.text: Trading algorithms execute buy and sell orders based on mathematical models.

discovery.text: AI models now predict market movements using satellite imagery, social media sentiment, and shipping data.

twist.text: Algorithmic trading creates flash crashes when models trigger chain reactions.

climax.text: The trading floor went from crowded and loud to quiet and algorithmic.

punchline.text: 600 traders became 2. Algorithms replaced the trading floor.

quiz.question: How did Goldman Sachs' equity trading staff change from 2000 to 2020?
options: It went from 600 traders to just 2 as algorithms took over

details.summary: Banks use algorithms to execute trades automatically based on predefined strategies, analyzing market data and executing orders in milliseconds. Algorithmic trading now accounts for the majority of trading volume in major financial markets.
details.whyItMatters: Algorithms have transformed banking from a relationship business to a technology arms race. Banks that invest in better algorithms gain massive advantages in execution speed, accuracy, and cost efficiency over competitors.
takeaways: Algorithms execute the majority of trades in major financial markets
Banks invest billions in trading technology and infrastructure
Algorithmic errors can cause flash crashes and market disruptions

faq.question: What advantages do algorithms have over human traders?
faq.answer: Algorithms process market data and execute trades in microseconds, far faster than any human. They follow strategies without emotional bias, can monitor thousands of instruments simultaneously, and operate continuously without fatigue.

faq.question: What happens when trading algorithms malfunction?
faq.answer: Knight Capital lost 440 million dollars in 45 minutes due to a software bug in 2012. Algorithmic errors can cascade through markets as other algorithms react to abnormal prices, amplifying volatility before human intervention occurs.
